title: User Training
summary: User training is the deliberate programme of awareness, simulation, and reinforcement that changes how staff behave when they encounter social engineering, credential harvesting, or anomalous requests. It is implemented as more than an annual slide deck: mature organisations combine role-specific curricula, regular phishing simulations with per-department reporting metrics, a genuinely frictionless report-phishing button wired into the security operations queue, and targeted deep-dive sessions for high-risk populations such as finance, executives, help desk, and developers. The control matters because the overwhelming majority of intrusions still begin with a human decision, and because trained users become a detection source rather than only a victim population. Well-run programmes shorten the time between a lure landing and an analyst investigating, which directly reduces dwell time. It breaks spearphishing behaviours, including attachment and link variants, and it degrades follow-on actions such as user execution and credential submission to attacker infrastructure. The honest limitations are significant. Training decays quickly without reinforcement, simulation results are easily gamed by anxious staff who report everything or by teams that game click rates, and no amount of awareness defeats a well-crafted pretext aimed at a tired employee at the end of a quarter. Training also shifts blame toward users when the real failure is missing technical control: an organisation with no multi-factor authentication, no attachment sandboxing, and no egress filtering should not treat awareness as its primary defence. Failure modes include measuring completion rather than behaviour, running simulations that punish reporting, ignoring the report queue so that employees learn their reports go nowhere, and delivering generic content that never reflects the actual lures targeting the sector.
objectives: Explain how to design a role-specific security awareness curriculum and measure behavioural change rather than course completion.
Describe how to run phishing simulations ethically and use reporting rate and time-to-report as operational metrics.
Explain how a report-phishing workflow should connect end users to the security operations queue and what triage must look like.
Identify the high-risk populations that warrant targeted deep-dive training and the scenarios most relevant to each.
Describe how awareness failure modes such as blame culture and unreviewed reports undermine the control.
Explain why user training must be paired with technical controls such as multi-factor authentication and attachment handling to be credible.
Evaluate training programme results against phishing-resistant control gaps and recommend a sequenced remediation plan.

beginner.definition: User training is a planned programme that teaches staff how attackers trick people and what to do about it. It goes beyond one yearly slide show. It includes role-specific lessons, realistic practice messages, and an easy way to report anything suspicious. Its goal is to turn employees into extra eyes, not just possible victims.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most intrusions still begin when a person opens a file, clicks a link, or approves a login. Technology cannot catch every trick. Trained staff notice odd requests and report them quickly, which shortens the time an attacker can stay hidden. Training also spreads good habits across the whole company, so one careless click is less likely to become a serious breach.
howItWorks: The team writes lessons for each job role, because finance, help desk, and engineers face different tricks.
Staff receive realistic practice messages and learn to spot pressure, odd senders, and unexpected links.
A single report button sits in the mail client and sends suspicious messages straight to the security team.
Analysts review every report and tell the reporter what they found, so people trust the process.
Leaders track how fast people report, not just how many finish the course.
Short refreshers run through the year, and high-risk groups get deeper sessions.
beginner.example: Imagine a neighbourhood watch. One alert resident who calls the police is useful. A whole street that knows what to look for is far better. They learn that a stranger claiming to read the meter should show a badge, and they ring a neighbour before opening the door. Security training works the same way. You learn the usual stories, you check before you act, and you tell someone quickly when something feels wrong.
takeaways: Train people to report, not to feel blamed for every message.
Measure how fast reports arrive, and not only how many courses finish.
Pair training with technical controls, because awareness alone cannot stop everything.
